source_reviews.independent_solution: Diffusion is spontaneous mutual mixing associated with irregular microscopic motion. An observable liquid experiment needs liquids in contact, an initially distinguishable concentration/color boundary, minimal initial bulk mixing, no stirring, and observation of gradual boundary spreading. Carefully putting denser colored sugar solution below gently added water can provide such a qualitative setup. Stable layering and stillness reduce bulk motion but do not prove convection absent. A definition alone is not a report of designing or performing this experiment. No actual result or duration was obtained by this reviewer. This was recorded before opening the draft.

source_reviews.independent_solution: In salting foods, dissolved salt constituents can redistribute toward accessible lower-salt water within food. This is a diffusion contribution, distinct from pressure-driven bulk liquid flow. Water transfer, including osmosis where a selectively permeable barrier applies, and tissue changes can coexist. Neither all preservation effects nor every water movement is just simple diffusion. For an initial outside-high/inside-low salt comparison, ordinary net diffusion reduces the difference rather than increasing it. This source analysis predates the candidate.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Atmospheric gases can dissolve at the water surface; dissolved molecules continue random motion and, with a relevant concentration difference, can spread into adjacent and deeper water by diffusion. Local random trajectories are not straight paths to the bottom. Diffusive transport becomes slow over large distances; bulk water flow and convection can move dissolved gases, and consumption or layering can limit bottom concentration. Diffusion alone cannot unconditionally guarantee rapid supply or uniform gas content at an arbitrary bottom. This distinction was saved in the blind record, without consulting textbook answers.
